en.html:
One theory says Yamato's spear arrived from the continent during the Mongol invasions. In time it snatched the top place among long-handled weapons from the naginata, and boomed all the way through the warring-states age.

If that is true, it means one thing: the spear simply had the advantage.

Standing against one now, I understood the reason perfectly. Disgustingly well.

The enemy armor was slow on its feet.

Even I, who had not yet got used to flying Masamune, could grab the high ground exactly by the iron rule of futawagakari. Next to Minato's Muramasa, this thing was a tortoise.

So the advantage in the tachiuchi was settled. Height makes speed, speed makes force. Basic.

But all of that—

en.html:
Same reason a warrior flying at speed relied on cuts, not thrusts.

A point was harder to land. A line gave you much more to hit with.

Sure, a spear let you attack from outside the enemy’s reach. Wonderful—provided the thrust landed. That was at least as difficult as hitting with a sword thrust. Harder, with all that extra length.

Miss once, and the enemy was inside your guard. Then what could the spear do? Nothing. Your turn to be cut up without getting a blow back.

Thinking could wait.

Now I had to concentrate.

Even after getting somewhat used to it, reading that spearhead demanded ferocious focus. It was not work to do with a wandering mind.

And the opponent was, from every angle, the crookedest of the crooked: more twists in him than a ghat road. Now that I had read him once, he was sure to add one.

Even so—
